newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Oprah Winfrey book club creates best-sellers.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Oprah Winfrey book club creates best-sellers.

text.p: Please Oprah, read my book.
The next author Oprah Winfrey picks for her televised "book club" is almost guaranteed a spot on the best-seller lists.

After Winfrey launched her crusade to get Americans to read by recommending Jacquelyn Mitchard's little-known novel, "Deep End of the Ocean," on her Sept. 19 show, publisher Viking rushed out 850,000 hardcover copies of the heart-wrenching tale, which had previously sold a respectable 100,000 copies, sending it to the top of the New York Times best-seller list for six weeks.

She subsequently touted Toni Morrison's "Song of Solomon," first published in 1977, and exposed thousands of white middle-class homemakers to a brand of fiction wholly new to them. Publishers printed up hundreds of thousands of hardback and paperback copies of the book.
Her latest choice was Jane Hamilton's 1988 novel, "The Book of Ruth."

While publishers and authors treasure a favourable review in the New York Times, they say a mention in a popular magazine or on a TV talk show can do more to boost sales. And Winfrey's impact on the publishing industry has been unprecedented because of the extent of her reach and her reputation for earnest, heartfelt honesty.

"I trust her opinion on things," Heather Mataya, 35, a Springfield, Illinois, mother of five, said. "She's very trustworthy, she's down to earth, she is what she says she is. She is as she appears to be on the show."
BREAKS NEW GROUND FOR READERS

Following the book club broadcasts, legions of Winfrey's 15-to-20 million viewers ventured out in search of her recommendations. Then, a month later, they tuned in to see the author gushed over, followed by video clips of a dinner with four lucky reader-viewers invited in for a discussion.

"I never ever would have picked up a book like this to read with its racial background," Mataya said of Morrison's work. "I love it." She said perusing the thousands of books available at a local bookstore usually left her baffled but "now I have titles to go in and buy."
If the books are still available.

Bookstores like Crown Books in downtown Chicago were swept clean of the first two titles within days of the broadcasts. Once publishers replenished stocks, many stores set up "as seen on Oprah" display racks.

"Anybody's book would do well," Crown bookstore manager Gonzalo Garcia said of the phenomenon, noting sales compared favourably with new offerings from established best-selling authors like John Grisham.

"The fact is, she's in a medium (television) that reaches people that don't get reached by books," said author Stuart Dybeck, who penned a short-story collection entitled "Coast of Chicago." Dybeck said he was curious when he spotted several straight-laced people engrossed in "Song of Solomon," but "now I know why."

He was less than hopeful that the star of talk TV would give his collection a glance but was glad of the exposure for well-written fiction. "She's not picking thrillers, pot-boilers, romances, self-help books or escapist literature. The level of choice is good. I'm amazed that her opinion has such an impact," he said.
CELEBRITY HELPS

He shouldn't be. Oprah Winfrey is viewed as perhaps America's most genuine celebrity and her credible-sounding opinions on diet and exercise have sold thousands of her own books as well. In the self-help book section, a slimmed-down Winfrey appears with her personal trainer on the book cover of "Make the Connection -- Ten Steps to a Better Body."
"She's an avid reader," her television show spokeswoman Audrey Pass said. "We've made clear we're not soliciting books; she wants to keep it pure and recommend books that have affected her."

With more than double the ratings of her nearest daytime talk competitor and big movie acting and producing credits, Winfrey clearly has a hold on a segment of the public consciousness. Her personal stories of growing up poor and abused in the South, wrestling with weight problems as an adult, then dealing humbly with enormous celebrity and massive wealth resonate with many people.

"She's great, she's smart, she doesn't insult anybody, she doesn't have weird people on the show," Angela Hutchens of Orange Park, Florida, said. "I can relate to her. I admire her, partly because she grew up in the South and I grew up in the South. You don't see people with that much money present themselves that way."

A 21-year-old part-time student, full-time worker and wife, Hutchens said she never misses an Oprah show and was unlikely to purchase a book recommended by anyone else. She remembered particularly a segment during the "book club" discussion when a wealthy woman said she could not relate to Morrison's novel, then broke down in tears in typical talk-show style as she realised the error of her ways.

"Eighty percent of readers in America are females," said Dr. Leonard Goldberg, a Los Angeles-based writer of medical thrillers such as "Deadly Care." "The reality is, all you need is a small percentage of these people sitting in front of their television sets to buy it and you're off and running."
